title: Before you were a thing
hook: was there a time when the human was nothing worth mentioning (76:1)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jibril, and don't hurry your tongue, and your line, don't hurry. Did someone get to finish their sentence before you spoke? Today a new surah, named for us: al-Insan, the Human. Day six hundred fifty-nine.

Find a photo from before you were born. Your parents' wedding, maybe, or a family picnic. Everyone's there, laughing, squinting into the sun. The world is going on, full of people and plans and weather. And you're nowhere. Not hiding, not waiting offstage. Just not yet. Nobody in the picture is thinking of you, because there is no you yet to think of. Surah seventy-six opens by asking us to think about it on purpose, with a question that isn't really a question.

Verse one, in Pickthall's translation: "Hath there come upon man (ever) any period of time in which he was a thing unremembered?" The Arabic phrase at the end is shay'an madhkura: a thing mentioned, a thing worth speaking of. There was a stretch of time, the verse says, when the human being wasn't even that. Not a name, not a memory, not a thought in anyone's head. Some commentators point out that the opening word, hal, usually a question, works here more like a statement: indeed, there came such a time. The answer is built into the asking. Of course there was. Then verse two moves fast: We created the human from a drop, mingled, to test him, and We made him hearing, seeing. From nothing worth mentioning, to a drop, to a listener and a watcher. And verse three: We showed him the way, whether he is grateful or ungrateful. The surah has a second name, ad-Dahr, Time, after this first verse. And it has a special place in the week. According to hadith in Bukhari and Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ would recite it, along with surah as-Sajdah, in the dawn prayer on Fridays, and some mosques keep that custom. Where they do, the congregation begins Friday by remembering it was once nothing. Why start there? Because it reframes everything that follows. If you were once not even a thing mentioned, then everything since, your breath, your name, the people in your life, the very ability to hear these words, arrived as a gift. Gratitude starts from zero.

The practice: think of before you were born. Sit, and picture the world a year before you arrived. The same sky, the same streets, maybe your parents young. You aren't in it. Stay with that for a few breaths, without fear. Then, slowly, add yourself back: your first breath, your name being said for the first time, your eyes opening, your ears hearing. Notice each one as something that arrived. The bell holds the time.
Ad-Dahr, Time: the surah's second name, after its opening question about a stretch when the human wasn't even a thing worth mentioning. Today's word.
Your line: once, nothing. Today, when you catch yourself taking something for granted, your hands, your hearing, a person, remember it wasn't always there. Day six hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Surah al-Insan (also called ad-Dahr) is recited in some mosques in the dawn prayer on Fridays, alongside as-Sajdah, following the Prophet's practice reported in Bukhari and Muslim.

fork.setup: the surah asks: was there a time when the human was nothing worth mentioning? what's the answer the verse builds in?
fork.reveal: the question is really a statement: indeed there was. then a drop, then hearing and seeing: everything since is a gift.

original.note: Arabic, 76:1: a thing mentioned, a thing worth speaking of.

trapdoor: what you thought: a question about where we came from.
what it means: the human was once nothing worth mentioning, then made hearing and seeing: a reason for gratitude.
what a scholar hears: some grammarians read hal here as qad, 'indeed'; the surah is also called ad-Dahr and was recited at Friday fajr.
